scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The bubble dance emerged in early 20th-century entertainment and gained defining recognition when performer Sally Rand popularized the solo stage act in the 1930s.
The routine featured a performer maneuvering a large spherical prop while dancing on stage before a live audience.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The performance served primarily as visual theatrical entertainment and erotic stage art within burlesque and revue contexts in the 1930s.
In social contexts, such as local community lodge dances held in hall venues during the 1920s, the name was associated with public social gatherings intended for community recreation.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The defining attire of the soloist in classic bubble dance performances is nudity, with the dancer relying on a large spherical prop shaped like a balloon or ball placed between herself and the spectators.
In contemporary 1930s film appearances and cartoon depictions, stage settings feature dramatic spotlighting, stage curtains, and proscenium framing that emphasize the soloist's movement.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Sally Rand is the central historical figure associated with the bubble dance, having brought the form to national fame in the 1930s.

Her performance was widely recognized and subsequently depicted in period motion pictures such as Sunset Murder Case (1938) and parodied in animated short films like Tex Avery's Hollywood Steps Out (1941).
The bubble dance is classified as a type of erotic stage dance.

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Bubble dance (United States). Mood: theatrical, sensual, playful. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.

Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
